findings.title: Negative (indefinite) ASN.1 length causes NegativeArraySizeException instead of IOException
findings.body: `ASN1Decoder.readLength()` returns `-1` when it encounters the indefinite-length byte `0x80` (lines 133-135). However, callers (`readSequence`, `readInteger`, and `readNext`) do not handle `-1` as an indefinite length: `readInteger()` passes `-1` directly to `read(length)` which throws `NegativeArraySizeException` on `new byte[length]`, and `readNext()` adds `reset()` (typically 2) to `-1` and reads 1 byte instead of failing, corrupting parsing or causing an infinite loop in `readSequence()`. Since DER encoding does not allow indefinite lengths (or if indefinite length is not supported), `readLength()` should throw an `IOException` when `length == 0x80`.

findings.title: ECDSAAlgorithmTest uses a single P-256 key for ES384 and ES512 and does not verify the re-encoded DER signature
findings.body: `ECDSAAlgorithmTest` generates a single default EC key pair (256-bit / P-256) in the constructor and reuses it across `testES256`, `testES384`, and `testES512`. Because the key is 256-bit, `signature.sign()` always produces ~64-byte R/S values (32 bytes each) even with `SHA384withECDSA` and `SHA512withECDSA`, so `testES384` (96-byte signatureLength) and `testES512` (132-byte signatureLength, where 66-byte R/S requires multi-byte DER length encoding > 127 bytes) never exercise full-size P-384 / P-521 signatures or long-form DER lengths. In addition, `test()` only checks that converting DER -> RS -> DER -> RS yields the same RS array, without verifying `asn1Des` against `Signature.verify(asn1Des)` to ensure the produced ASN.1 DER is accepted by the JCA `Signature` verifier.

findings.title: Unused ASN1Encoder allocations in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.body: Lines 114-115 call `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` and discard the returned encoders before immediately repeating the exact same calls inside `writeDerSeq(...)` on lines 119-120. Those two statements are dead code that allocate and populate `ByteArrayOutputStream` instances for nothing.
